cards.explanation: Laboratory and population information help identify emergence and spread.
cards.text: Biomedical scientists contribute to outbreak investigation through disease detection and {{c1::surveillance}}.
cards.question: Biomedical scientists contribute to outbreak investigation through disease detection and {{c1::surveillance}}.

cards.explanation: The emphasis is on patterns across populations and the factors influencing them, rather than only an individual diagnosis.
cards.text: Epidemiology studies the distribution of disease in {{c1::populations}}.
cards.question: Epidemiology studies the distribution of disease in {{c1::populations}}.

cards.explanation: Identifying how disease is distributed helps decide where prevention and control should be directed.
cards.text: Population-level epidemiological data inform {{c1::public health interventions}}.
cards.question: Population-level epidemiological data inform {{c1::public health interventions}}.

cards.explanation: The remaining links concern where it persists, how it leaves and reaches another host, and host susceptibility.
cards.text: In the chain of infection, the organism causing infection is the {{c1::infectious agent}}.
cards.question: In the chain of infection, the organism causing infection is the {{c1::infectious agent}}.

cards.explanation: Reservoirs may be human, animal or environmental; a transmission route describes movement rather than maintenance.
cards.text: The habitat that maintains an infectious agent is its {{c1::reservoir}}.
cards.question: The habitat that maintains an infectious agent is its {{c1::reservoir}}.

cards.explanation: The chain distinguishes exit from subsequent transmission and entry into a new host.
cards.text: The route by which an agent leaves its reservoir is its {{c1::portal of exit}}.
cards.question: The route by which an agent leaves its reservoir is its {{c1::portal of exit}}.

cards.explanation: Contact, respiratory and vector routes require different control measures.
cards.text: The link connecting a portal of exit to a new host is the {{c1::mode of transmission}}.
cards.question: The link connecting a portal of exit to a new host is the {{c1::mode of transmission}}.

cards.explanation: Entry is a separate link from the host’s susceptibility.
cards.text: The route by which an agent enters a new host is its {{c1::portal of entry}}.
cards.question: The route by which an agent enters a new host is its {{c1::portal of entry}}.

cards.explanation: Exposure does not have the same consequence in every person; immunity and other host factors matter.
cards.text: The final host-related link in the chain is a {{c1::susceptible host}}.
cards.question: The final host-related link in the chain is a {{c1::susceptible host}}.

cards.explanation: Effective interventions should target a link relevant to that pathogen and setting.
cards.text: Transmission can be interrupted by breaking {{c1::any link}} in the chain of infection.
cards.question: Transmission can be interrupted by breaking {{c1::any link}} in the chain of infection.

cards.explanation: The lecture’s diagram shows this before the prodromal stage. Lack of symptoms does not necessarily mean lack of infectiousness.
cards.text: The interval after exposure before signs or symptoms develop is the {{c1::incubation period}}.
cards.question: The interval after exposure before signs or symptoms develop is the {{c1::incubation period}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram distinguishes this from the later period of more severe illness.
cards.text: The stage with early mild signs or symptoms is the {{c1::prodromal period}}.
cards.question: The stage with early mild signs or symptoms is the {{c1::prodromal period}}.

cards.explanation: The curve is a schematic disease course, not a universal quantitative pathogen-load measurement.
cards.text: The most severe signs and symptoms occur during the diagram’s {{c1::period of illness}}.
cards.question: The most severe signs and symptoms occur during the diagram’s {{c1::period of illness}}.

cards.explanation: Declining symptoms are followed by convalescence; they do not alone establish that transmission has stopped.
cards.text: The stage in which signs and symptoms start to subside is the period of {{c1::decline}}.
cards.question: The stage in which signs and symptoms start to subside is the period of {{c1::decline}}.

cards.explanation: This is the final named period in the lecture’s disease-progression sequence.
cards.text: Recovery after the decline stage is called {{c1::convalescence}}.
cards.question: Recovery after the decline stage is called {{c1::convalescence}}.

cards.explanation: The infectious period and symptomatic period need not coincide; timing depends on the pathogen.
cards.text: For some infections, transmission can occur {{c1::before symptoms begin}}.
cards.question: For some infections, transmission can occur {{c1::before symptoms begin}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s vomiting/diarrhoea poster illustrates pathogen-specific exclusion advice; its 48-hour rule is not a rule for every infection.
cards.text: Resolution of symptoms does {{c1::not necessarily end infectiousness}}.
cards.question: Resolution of symptoms does {{c1::not necessarily end infectiousness}}.

cards.explanation: Such a person may be unaware of the infection and still contribute to spread.
cards.text: An infected person who transmits an agent without symptoms is an {{c1::asymptomatic carrier}}.
cards.question: An infected person who transmits an agent without symptoms is an {{c1::asymptomatic carrier}}.

cards.explanation: This helps explain why some outbreaks are difficult to detect and control.
cards.text: Control based only on recognising symptomatic people can miss {{c1::asymptomatic carriers}}.
cards.question: Control based only on recognising symptomatic people can miss {{c1::asymptomatic carriers}}.

cards.explanation: The illustrated study concerns sexually transmitted enteric infections. Its acceptability findings help evaluate how feasible surveillance is; they are not infection-prevalence estimates.
cards.text: In the pilot-study infographic, flexible sampling that fits a daily routine {{c1::facilitated participation}}.
cards.question: In the pilot-study infographic, flexible sampling that fits a daily routine {{c1::facilitated participation}}.

cards.explanation: Participants requested clearer information about this requirement. This is a study-specific barrier, not a universal statement about every surveillance programme.
cards.text: The pilot-study infographic identifies completing {{c1::weekly questionnaires}} as the most challenging aspect.
cards.question: The pilot-study infographic identifies completing {{c1::weekly questionnaires}} as the most challenging aspect.

cards.explanation: Infection can be maintained across interconnected settings, so investigating only humans may miss an important source.
cards.text: The One Health approach connects human, animal and {{c1::environmental}} reservoirs.
cards.question: The One Health approach connects human, animal and {{c1::environmental}} reservoirs.

cards.explanation: The lecture highlights the role of such reservoirs in emerging infections.
cards.text: An animal reservoir relevant to human infection is a {{c1::zoonotic reservoir}}.
cards.question: An animal reservoir relevant to human infection is a {{c1::zoonotic reservoir}}.

cards.explanation: The slide separately names protozoa and other parasites; not every infectious agent is a bacterium or virus.
cards.text: Infectious agents include prions as well as bacteria, viruses, fungi and {{c1::parasites}}.
cards.question: Infectious agents include prions as well as bacteria, viruses, fungi and {{c1::parasites}}.

cards.explanation: The slide lists this separately from vectors. Food and water in the later plenary illustrate possible common media; the exact exposure pattern determines outbreak type.
cards.text: Transmission through a contaminated common medium is described as {{c1::vehicle-borne}} transmission.
cards.question: Transmission through a contaminated common medium is described as {{c1::vehicle-borne}} transmission.

cards.explanation: This differs from transfer through a contaminated object.
cards.text: Physical interaction between individuals is {{c1::direct contact transmission}}.
cards.question: Physical interaction between individuals is {{c1::direct contact transmission}}.

cards.explanation: An object such as a shared handle is a potential fomite; the picture alone does not show that it is contaminated.
cards.text: Transfer through a contaminated surface or object is {{c1::indirect contact transmission}}.
cards.question: Transfer through a contaminated surface or object is {{c1::indirect contact transmission}}.

cards.explanation: It limits transfer on hands; it should not be assumed to control every respiratory or vector route by itself.
cards.text: Hand hygiene helps interrupt {{c1::contact transmission}}.
cards.question: Hand hygiene helps interrupt {{c1::contact transmission}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture uses this distinction to explain why respiratory control measures can differ. Actual respiratory particles form a continuum rather than two perfectly separate categories.
cards.text: Compared with larger droplets, airborne particles can remain {{c1::suspended for longer}}.
cards.question: Compared with larger droplets, airborne particles can remain {{c1::suspended for longer}}.

cards.explanation: This is a general comparison with suspended airborne particles, not a precise safe-distance cut-off.
cards.text: In the lecture’s contrast, larger respiratory droplets generally settle over {{c1::shorter distances}}.
cards.question: In the lecture’s contrast, larger respiratory droplets generally settle over {{c1::shorter distances}}.

cards.explanation: Measures suited to contact alone may be insufficient when inhalation is important.
cards.text: Choosing respiratory infection-control measures requires knowing the {{c1::transmission route}}.
cards.question: Choosing respiratory infection-control measures requires knowing the {{c1::transmission route}}.

cards.explanation: Vectors transmit agents between hosts; the lecture’s diagram links different vectors with different diseases.
cards.text: Mosquitoes, ticks and fleas can act as infectious-disease {{c1::vectors}}.
cards.question: Mosquitoes, ticks and fleas can act as infectious-disease {{c1::vectors}}.

cards.explanation: Where vectors can survive and contact hosts influences where transmission can occur.
cards.text: Vector ecology helps determine the geographical {{c1::distribution of vector-borne disease}}.
cards.question: Vector ecology helps determine the geographical {{c1::distribution of vector-borne disease}}.

cards.explanation: Host immunity is one contributor to susceptibility, alongside exposure and pathogen factors.
cards.text: Compared with an immunocompetent host, an immunocompromised host generally has {{c1::higher infection risk}}.
cards.question: Compared with an immunocompetent host, an immunocompromised host generally has {{c1::higher infection risk}}.

cards.explanation: The same exposure can therefore carry different risks for different people.
cards.text: Age, genetics, nutrition and underlying disease modify {{c1::host susceptibility}}.
cards.question: Age, genetics, nutrition and underlying disease modify {{c1::host susceptibility}}.

cards.explanation: Endemic describes expected ongoing occurrence; it does not mean the disease is harmless.
cards.text: A disease maintained at a predictable background level in an area is {{c1::endemic}}.
cards.question: A disease maintained at a predictable background level in an area is {{c1::endemic}}.

cards.explanation: This is the lecture’s operational definition. In practice, a single unusual or high-consequence case may also trigger an outbreak investigation; do not use two cases as a universal reporting threshold.
cards.text: The lecture defines an outbreak as at least two cases linked by time, place or {{c1::common exposure}}.
cards.question: The lecture defines an outbreak as at least two cases linked by time, place or {{c1::common exposure}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts a larger affected area with a local outbreak; the key comparison is with the expected baseline.
cards.text: Disease occurrence above the expected level in a population over a period is an {{c1::epidemic}}.
cards.question: Disease occurrence above the expected level in a population over a period is an {{c1::epidemic}}.

cards.explanation: Pandemic describes geographical spread and transmission, not necessarily greater severity in each infected person.
cards.text: Widespread international disease transmission above expected occurrence is a {{c1::pandemic}}.
cards.question: Widespread international disease transmission above expected occurrence is a {{c1::pandemic}}.

cards.explanation: The purpose includes early detection and an evidence-based public health response.
cards.text: Continuous monitoring of disease occurrence is {{c1::disease surveillance}}.
cards.question: Continuous monitoring of disease occurrence is {{c1::disease surveillance}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture gives examples, but its list is not a complete or permanently current legal list.
cards.text: A disease subject to a legal reporting requirement is a {{c1::notifiable disease}}.
cards.question: A disease subject to a legal reporting requirement is a {{c1::notifiable disease}}.

cards.explanation: UK Health Security Agency. Reporting arrangements vary across UK nations; the linked GOV.UK guidance is the relevant source for current English requirements.
cards.text: The agency named for collating the lecture’s surveillance data is {{c1::UKHSA}}.
cards.question: The agency named for collating the lecture’s surveillance data is {{c1::UKHSA}}.

cards.explanation: The warning concerns the clinician’s notification on suspicion under the applicable reporting system; laboratory reporting duties are distinct.
cards.text: The reporting warning on slide 19 says not to wait for {{c1::laboratory confirmation}} of a suspected notifiable disease.
cards.question: The reporting warning on slide 19 says not to wait for {{c1::laboratory confirmation}} of a suspected notifiable disease.

cards.explanation: These illustrate the category; checking current jurisdiction-specific guidance is preferable to memorising the slide as an exhaustive legal list.
cards.text: Measles and cholera are examples of {{c1::notifiable diseases}} in the lecture.
cards.question: Measles and cholera are examples of {{c1::notifiable diseases}} in the lecture.

cards.explanation: This is an early loss in the surveillance pyramid, before testing or reporting.
cards.text: Surveillance may miss infected people because some do not {{c1::seek medical attention}}.
cards.question: Surveillance may miss infected people because some do not {{c1::seek medical attention}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture notes that clinical diagnoses may be made without laboratory confirmation.
cards.text: A person attending healthcare may still be absent from laboratory-confirmed counts if they are {{c1::not tested}}.
cards.question: A person attending healthcare may still be absent from laboratory-confirmed counts if they are {{c1::not tested}}.

cards.explanation: Care-seeking, testing and reporting each affect the relationship between recorded and true infections.
cards.text: Even a confirmed infection may be absent from surveillance if it is {{c1::not reported}}.
cards.question: Even a confirmed infection may be absent from surveillance if it is {{c1::not reported}}.

cards.explanation: Application of the surveillance pyramid: changing detection can change reported counts. Compare ascertainment as well as the case total.
cards.text: An increase in testing can raise recorded case numbers without necessarily proving {{c1::increased transmission}}.
cards.question: An increase in testing can raise recorded case numbers without necessarily proving {{c1::increased transmission}}.

cards.explanation: Incidence describes new disease acquisition rather than all people currently infected.
cards.text: The measure based on new cases arising during a defined period is {{c1::incidence}}.
cards.question: The measure based on new cases arising during a defined period is {{c1::incidence}}.

cards.explanation: Worked interpretation: 50/1,000 × 100. This is an incidence proportion over the stated period, not a person-time incidence rate.
cards.text: The lecture’s 50 new infections among 1,000 initially at-risk students in one week represent a one-week risk of {{c1::5%}}.
cards.question: The lecture’s 50 new infections among 1,000 initially at-risk students in one week represent a one-week risk of {{c1::5%}}.

cards.explanation: The example “50 students are currently infected today” describes existing cases, not necessarily 50 new infections.
cards.text: The number or proportion of people with an existing infection at a specified time is {{c1::point prevalence}}.
cards.question: The number or proportion of people with an existing infection at a specified time is {{c1::point prevalence}}.

cards.explanation: Incidence instead focuses on new cases and acquisition over time.
cards.text: Prevalence reflects the current {{c1::disease burden}} in a population.
cards.question: Prevalence reflects the current {{c1::disease burden}} in a population.

cards.explanation: Longer-lasting disease can keep people in the pool of existing cases for longer.
cards.text: Besides incidence, prevalence is influenced by disease {{c1::duration}}.
cards.question: Besides incidence, prevalence is influenced by disease {{c1::duration}}.

cards.explanation: A count alone does not give the proportion affected. This distinguishes the slide’s count from a population prevalence percentage.
cards.text: “50 students are currently infected” cannot be converted into a prevalence percentage without the {{c1::population denominator}}.
cards.question: “50 students are currently infected” cannot be converted into a prevalence percentage without the {{c1::population denominator}}.

cards.explanation: Despite the name, this is a proportion over the outbreak period; define the exposed or at-risk population being counted.
cards.text: The proportion becoming ill during a defined outbreak is the {{c1::attack rate}}.
cards.question: The proportion becoming ill during a defined outbreak is the {{c1::attack rate}}.

cards.explanation: It concerns new cases among susceptible contacts of initial cases, rather than simply the total cases in an entire population.
cards.text: The measure focusing on spread to household or other close contacts is the {{c1::secondary attack rate}}.
cards.question: The measure focusing on spread to household or other close contacts is the {{c1::secondary attack rate}}.

cards.explanation: The question concerns onward transmission to close contacts, not just who is infected at one time.
cards.text: To assess spread within households after an initial case, choose the {{c1::secondary attack rate}} rather than population point prevalence.
cards.question: To assess spread within households after an initial case, choose the {{c1::secondary attack rate}} rather than population point prevalence.

cards.explanation: The slide states the average-secondary-case definition. Fully susceptible conditions distinguish basic R₀ from an effective reproduction number under current immunity or interventions.
cards.text: R₀ is the average number of {{c1::secondary cases}} generated by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population.
cards.question: R₀ is the average number of {{c1::secondary cases}} generated by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population.

cards.explanation: Each infection produces more than one new infection on average. This is a population tendency, not a promise that every introduction causes a large outbreak.
cards.text: A reproduction number greater than 1 supports {{c1::growth in transmission}}.
cards.question: A reproduction number greater than 1 supports {{c1::growth in transmission}}.

cards.explanation: Each infection generates fewer than one further infection on average. It does not mean transmission stops immediately.
cards.text: A reproduction number below 1 implies transmission tends to {{c1::decline}}.
cards.question: A reproduction number below 1 implies transmission tends to {{c1::decline}}.

cards.explanation: The pattern can suggest exposure and transmission dynamics during an outbreak.
cards.text: An epidemic curve plots case numbers against {{c1::time}}.
cards.question: An epidemic curve plots case numbers against {{c1::time}}.

cards.explanation: Combine the pattern with exposure histories, testing and other investigation evidence.
cards.text: An epidemic curve can suggest a source pattern but cannot alone {{c1::prove the source}}.
cards.question: An epidemic curve can suggest a source pattern but cannot alone {{c1::prove the source}}.

cards.explanation: The schematic shows a concentrated peak, unlike prolonged exposure or successive transmission waves.
cards.text: A single brief common exposure produces a {{c1::point-source outbreak}}.
cards.question: A single brief common exposure produces a {{c1::point-source outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: The schematic has sustained cases over a broader period.
cards.text: Prolonged exposure to the same source produces a {{c1::continuous common-source outbreak}}.
cards.question: Prolonged exposure to the same source produces a {{c1::continuous common-source outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: Successive generations may produce waves rather than one common-exposure peak.
cards.text: An outbreak sustained by person-to-person spread is {{c1::propagated}}.
cards.question: An outbreak sustained by person-to-person spread is {{c1::propagated}}.

cards.explanation: The illustrated cases form separated peaks. Intermittent exposure need not be truly random.
cards.text: Repeated but non-continuous exposure to a source gives an {{c1::intermittent common-source outbreak}}.
cards.question: Repeated but non-continuous exposure to a source gives an {{c1::intermittent common-source outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: Compare observed occurrence with what is expected and assess the evidence. The diagram also separates finding cases from verifying diagnoses.
cards.text: Before attributing a case cluster to an outbreak, first {{c1::confirm the outbreak}}.
cards.question: Before attributing a case cluster to an outbreak, first {{c1::confirm the outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: The illustrated framework includes defining cases before finding and describing them; consistency makes comparisons meaningful.
cards.text: A consistent {{c1::case definition}} helps investigators decide which people to count.
cards.question: A consistent {{c1::case definition}} helps investigators decide which people to count.

cards.explanation: An apparent association or plausible source is a starting explanation, not proof.
cards.text: A proposed source or route should be investigated by developing and {{c1::testing hypotheses}}.
cards.question: A proposed source or route should be investigated by developing and {{c1::testing hypotheses}}.

cards.explanation: The framework places tracing alongside transmission mapping, communication and control.
cards.text: Identifying people exposed to an infectious case is {{c1::contact tracing}}.
cards.question: Identifying people exposed to an infectious case is {{c1::contact tracing}}.

cards.explanation: The framework is iterative: check whether transmission is being reduced rather than assuming an intervention worked.
cards.text: After implementing control measures, investigators should {{c1::monitor and evaluate}} the response.
cards.question: After implementing control measures, investigators should {{c1::monitor and evaluate}} the response.

cards.explanation: The lecture reports close-contact behaviours and a targeted MenB vaccine response in March 2026. Its case totals are a dated source snapshot, not live surveillance data.
cards.text: The Kent MenB case study illustrates targeted {{c1::vaccination}} as an outbreak-control measure.
cards.question: The Kent MenB case study illustrates targeted {{c1::vaccination}} as an outbreak-control measure.

cards.explanation: This means healthcare acquisition, not merely that an infection is diagnosed while a person is in hospital.
cards.text: An infection acquired in hospital is termed {{c1::nosocomial}}.
cards.question: An infection acquired in hospital is termed {{c1::nosocomial}}.

cards.explanation: Healthcare settings combine susceptible hosts with repeated contacts and procedures.
cards.text: Vulnerable patients and opportunities for transmission make hospital {{c1::infection surveillance and control}} essential.
cards.question: Vulnerable patients and opportunities for transmission make hospital {{c1::infection surveillance and control}} essential.

cards.explanation: This targets the host-susceptibility link in the chain of infection.
cards.text: Vaccination can reduce the number of {{c1::susceptible hosts}}.
cards.question: Vaccination can reduce the number of {{c1::susceptible hosts}}.

cards.explanation: This can protect vulnerable people, but its strength depends on the pathogen, vaccine and population; it is not guaranteed individual protection.
cards.text: Indirect protection when transmission is reduced in a sufficiently immune population is {{c1::herd immunity}}.
cards.question: Indirect protection when transmission is reduced in a sufficiently immune population is {{c1::herd immunity}}.

cards.explanation: This is a population mechanism connecting vaccination coverage with transmission.
cards.text: Falling vaccine uptake can promote outbreaks by increasing the pool of {{c1::susceptible people}}.
cards.question: Falling vaccine uptake can promote outbreaks by increasing the pool of {{c1::susceptible people}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture also identifies pathogen evolution and antimicrobial resistance as contributors to emergence or re-emergence.
cards.text: Global travel facilitates rapid geographical {{c1::dissemination of infections}}.
cards.question: Global travel facilitates rapid geographical {{c1::dissemination of infections}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture connects AMR with emerging and re-emerging infections; resistance does not automatically mean intrinsically faster transmission.
cards.text: Resistance that makes infections harder to control is {{c1::antimicrobial resistance (AMR)}}.
cards.question: Resistance that makes infections harder to control is {{c1::antimicrobial resistance (AMR)}}.

cards.explanation: Patient and exposure information provide context for genetic relationships between sampled organisms.
cards.text: Genomic epidemiology combines population epidemiology with {{c1::pathogen genomic data}}.
cards.question: Genomic epidemiology combines population epidemiology with {{c1::pathogen genomic data}}.

cards.explanation: The labelled rings include year, sex, age and travel. The slide does not provide a spoken interpretation or isolate-level dataset, so no exact transmission chain is inferred.
cards.text: The circular figure combines a pathogen tree with patient and travel {{c1::metadata}}.
cards.question: The circular figure combines a pathogen tree with patient and travel {{c1::metadata}}.

cards.explanation: Examples labelled include blaCTX-M-27 and mph(A). The slide provides no complete susceptibility results or isolate-level identities; do not infer an individual treatment choice from the picture.
cards.text: The green presence/absence tracks in the genomic figure annotate {{c1::resistance-associated genetic markers}}.
cards.question: The green presence/absence tracks in the genomic figure annotate {{c1::resistance-associated genetic markers}}.

cards.explanation: Genetic relatedness alone does not identify who infected whom; the figure lacks a confirmed contact chain or detailed sampling account.
cards.text: A genetic tree should be interpreted alongside {{c1::epidemiological evidence}} when assessing a suspected transmission link.
cards.question: A genetic tree should be interpreted alongside {{c1::epidemiological evidence}} when assessing a suspected transmission link.

cards.explanation: This is a conditional answer to the plenary image. A buffet photograph alone does not establish exposure timing or prove contamination.
cards.text: Illness following a single shared buffet meal could produce a {{c1::point-source outbreak}}.
cards.question: Illness following a single shared buffet meal could produce a {{c1::point-source outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: The pump image alone does not show duration; the sustained-exposure assumption is what distinguishes this pattern.
cards.text: A water supply contaminated continuously over several days could produce a {{c1::continuous common-source outbreak}}.
cards.question: A water supply contaminated continuously over several days could produce a {{c1::continuous common-source outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: The pictured coughing group is a prompt for a possible route, not proof that this pattern occurred.
cards.text: Successive waves of illness due to transmission between classmates suggest a {{c1::propagated outbreak}}.
cards.question: Successive waves of illness due to transmission between classmates suggest a {{c1::propagated outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: The chef picture has no exposure timeline or answer key. Separate contamination episodes are an explicit revision scenario; a single meal would instead support point-source exposure.
cards.text: An infected food handler contaminating meals on separate occasions could produce an {{c1::intermittent common-source outbreak}}.
cards.question: An infected food handler contaminating meals on separate occasions could produce an {{c1::intermittent common-source outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: This integrates reservoirs, susceptibility and opportunities for transmission rather than attributing an outbreak to one factor alone.
cards.text: Disease spread depends on interactions between the pathogen, the host and the {{c1::environment}}.
cards.question: Disease spread depends on interactions between the pathogen, the host and the {{c1::environment}}.

slides.text:
LS5008 / LS5030
Epidemiology and Infection Spread
Dr Lewis C. E. Mason 
BSc (Hons), MSc, PhD, MSRB, FIBMS, AFHEA

Starter Activity
•
What do all these images have in common?

Learning objectives
•
Recall the terminology used in infectious
disease surveillance
•
Explain infectious disease timelines, cycles of
infection, and factors that play a role in each
stage
•
Critically evaluate methods and 
recommendations for controlling infectious disease

Why do we study epidemiology?
•
Infectious diseases remain a major
cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide
•
Epidemiology helps identify how 
diseases emerge, spread, and can be 
controlled
•
Biomedical scientists contribute to 
detection, surveillance, and outbreak 
investigation

What is epidemiology?
•
The study of the distribution of disease
in populations
•
Investigation of factors influencing
health and disease
•
Use of population-level data to inform
public health interventions

The Chain of Infection
•
The infectious agent itself, its reservoir(s),
portal of exit, transmission route, portal
of entry, and the susceptibility of the 
host
•
Disease spread can be interrupted 
at any stage
•
Public health interventions target specific
links in the chain

Disease Progression
• Exposure 
• Incubation period
• Prodromal period
• Illness period
• Decline
• Convalescence period

When are patients actually infectious?
• Infectiousness varies over the 
course of an infectious disease
• Transmission can occur before 
or even after the end of symptoms
• Pathogen characteristics
determine the length and
time of the infectious period

Asymptomatic carriers of infectious agents
• Asymptomatic carriers can
transmit pathogens without knowing
that they are infected 
• Carriers may contribute significantly
to outbreaks
• Public health control in these
cases can be very challenging

Infectious Agents and Reservoirs
•
Pathogens may be bacterial, viral, 
fungal, protozoal, parasitic, or prion
•
Human, animal, and environmental 
reservoirs can maintain infection
(One Health)
•
Zoonotic reservoirs play important
roles in emerging diseases

Routes of Transmission
•
Direct contact, indirect contact,
droplet, airborne, vehicle-borne,
and vector-borne transmission exists
•
Different pathogens exploit different
transmission routes
•
Understanding transmission guides
control measures

Direct and Indirect Contact Transmission
•
Direct contact requires physical
interaction between individuals
•
Indirect transmission occurs via
contaminated surfaces or objects
•
Hand hygiene remains an important
intervention!

Droplet vs Airborne Transmission
•
Droplets generally travel short distances before settling. Airborne 
particles can remain suspended for longer periods. Control 
measures differ substantially between the two routes

Vector-Borne Transmission
•
Mosquitos, ticks, and fleas are important vectors of infectious 
agents. Vector ecology strongly influences disease distribution

Susceptible Hosts and Risk Factors
•
Host immunity influences
infection risk
•
Age, genetics, nutrition, and
underlying disease are important
factors
•
Immunocompromised individuals 
are at higher risk of infection

Endemic, Outbreak, Epidemic, & Pandemic
•
Endemic diseases occur at predictable
background levels in an area over time
•
Outbreaks are: ‘an incident in which
at least two or more people are affected
by the same infectious disease, linked
by time, place, or common exposure’
•
Epidemics involve disease 
occurrence above expected levels
across a large area in a set amount of time
•
Pandemics involve widespread international transmission of a disease 
in greater numbers than expected over a set time period

Introduction to Disease Surveillance
•
There is a continuous monitoring of
disease occurrence for many diseases 
in the UK
•
It is a legal requirement for some
diseases to be reported: notifiable diseases
•
These data are collated by the UK Health
Security Agency (UKHSA), 
enabling early detection of outbreaks
•
All of this supports evidence-based
public health responses

Notifiable Diseases (some examples)
https://www.gov.uk/guidance/notifiable-diseases-and-how-to-
report-them#reporting-other-infectious-diseases
Anthrax
Botulism
Chickenpox
Cholera
Food poisoning
Diphtheria
Enteric fever
Malaria
Measles
Mpox
Mumps
Plague
Rabies
Infectious 
bloody diarrhoea

How effective is reporting?
•
Not every infected individual
seeks medical attention
•
Not every patient is tested,
clinical diagnosis may be
made without lab
confirmation
•
Not every confirmed case
is reported

Measuring disease frequency
•
Epidemiology partially relies on
quantitative measurements
•
‘Incidence’ and ‘Prevalence’ 
answer different questions
•
Accurate data collection is 
essential and makes inferences 
more powerful

Incidence
•
Measures new cases
arising over a specific period
of time 
•
Indicates current risk of
disease acquisition 
•
Useful for studying transmission
dynamics
•
E.g. ‘50 new cases among 1,000 students during one week’

Prevalence
•
Measures all existing cases
at a specific time point
•
Reflects disease burden
within a population
•
Influenced by both incidence 
and disease duration
•
E.g. ‘50 students are currently infected
today’

Attack Rate and Secondary Attack Rate
•
Frequently used 
during outbreak investigations
•
‘Attack rate’ estimates the
proportion becoming ill
•
Secondary attack rate 
assesses household or
close-contact spread

Basic Reproduction Number (R₀)
•
This is the average number of
 secondary cases caused by 
one infected individual
•
R₀ > 1     = Potential spread
•
R₀ < 1     = Declining 
                     transmission

Epidemic Curves
•
This is a visual representation
of cases over time
•
It can help to suggest 
source and transmission
patterns
•
A very important tool 
during outbreak investigations

Types of Outbreak
•
Point-source outbreaks arise from
a single exposure event
•
Continuous common-source 
outbreaks involve prolonged 
exposure
•
Propagated outbreaks involve
person-to-person transmission
•
Intermittent source outbreak is not constant, and seems random

Outbreak Investigation Process
• Confirm the outbreak
• Develop and test 
hypotheses
• Implement control 
measures and 
communicate findings

Case Study: Kent MenB Outbreak 
March 2026
•
The outbreak resulted
in 21 confirmed cases, 
9 of which requiring 
intensive care, & two deaths
•
Transmission driven by
kissing, sharing drinks,
and sharing vapes
•
Targeted menB vaccines
followed

Healthcare-Associated Infections
•
Hospitals provide ample
opportunities for pathogen
transmission
•
Infections that occur at a 
hospital are nosocomial 
•
Vulnerable patients are at
an increased risk
•
Surveillance and infection
control are absolutely essential
in hospitals

Vaccination and Herd Immunity
•
Vaccination reduces the number of susceptible hosts. Herd 
immunity protects vulnerable individuals. Declining vaccine 
uptake can promote outbreaks.

Emerging and Re-Emerging Infections
•
Pathogens continue to evolve and 
adapt
•
Global travel facilitates rapid 
dissemination
•
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) 
contributes to disease emergence

Genomic epidemiology
•
A combination of traditional
human-based population 
epidemiology alongside
genomics of the pathogen
•
Very powerful and increasingly
used to predict, identify,
and prevent outbreaks

Disease spread depends on
interactions between pathogen, host,

Epidemiology provides tools to

Surveillance and outbreak
